title: Outage: the file server's clock is ten minutes slow and logins fail

lines.text: 10:01 help desk: finance cannot open //files2/finance (Kerberos: clock skew too great)
10:31 payroll: the 10:30 run could not read the finance share
help desk: finance can open the share again

nodes.label: chronyd
nodes.status: {synced ? (confFixed ? "Synced to ntp1 (in chrony.conf)" : "Synced to ntp1 (added at run time only)") : "No usable source"}

nodes.label: System clock
nodes.status: {clockOk ? "Correct" : synced ? "580 s slow, slewing" : "580 s slow"}

objective: Configure time synchronization with chrony or systemd-timesyncd and check it with chronyc or timedatectl
secondaryObjectives: Troubleshoot networking with ip, ss, ping, tracepath, dig and the journal

sources.cite: Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator (LFCS): Domains & Competencies, Networking 25%
sources.note: Relevant text: Networking, 'Configure time synchronization service'. Read as the page's HTML on 2026-11-14 (page last modified 2026-10-30).

Relevant text: makestep 'forces chronyd to step the system clock if the adjustment is larger than a threshold value, but only if there were no more clock updates since chronyd was started than the specified limit' ('makestep 0.1 3' steps 'only in the first three clock updates'); 'By default, the maximum slew rate is set to 83333.333 ppm (one twelfth)'; iburst starts 'with a burst of 4-8 requests in order to make the first update of the clock sooner'. Read through a summarizing fetch 2026-11-14. At one twelfth, slewing out a 580 s error takes about 6,960 s: arithmetic from that default.

Relevant text: sources, '^ means a server'; '* indicates the best source which is currently selected for synchronisation'; '? indicates a source which is not considered to be selectable'; Reach '377 indicates that a valid reply was received for all from the last eight transmissions'. makestep (no arguments) 'tells chronyd to cancel any remaining correction that was being slewed and jump the system clock by the equivalent amount'. 'The add server command allows a new NTP server to be added whilst chronyd is running.' Read through summarizing fetches 2026-11-14. That a source added at run time is not written to chrony.conf, so a restart loses it, is inferred from chronyd reading its sources from the file at start.

Relevant text: clockskew 'Sets the maximum allowable amount of clockskew in seconds that the library will tolerate before assuming that a Kerberos message is invalid. The default value is 300 seconds, or five minutes.' Read through a summarizing fetch 2026-11-14. The smbclient error text is authored.

brief.situation: You look after files2, a Fedora-family file server that shares finance folders to domain users with Kerberos logins, for Alder Bay Credit Union (fictional). It was restored from last night's snapshot at 08:40 after a failed update. Since about 09:50 finance staff cannot open their share. Payroll reads the share at 10:30.
handover: The old time server, ntp-old.corp.example, was retired last month; the current ones are ntp1.corp.example and ntp2.corp.example.
chronyd on files2 has been running for 41 days on this image.
howItWorks: Run commands from the command line: type one, or pick it from the suggestions or the action list. Only this lab's commands run; there is no free shell, and each command's arguments are fixed.
Each command takes operator time: run it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The outage keeps developing on the same clock.
The map shows each host, disk or service and the links between them, with a status in words. Output appears in the terminal as it happens.
When you declare the service restored, you write the incident record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: How many operator minutes each command takes, and when the fictional outage spreads, are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values. Payroll reads the share at 10:30, about 30 minutes after the start.

effects.finding: chronyd is running but the clock is not synchronized.

sources.label: chronyc sources
sources.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

else.output:
[root@files2 ~]# chronyc sources
MS Name/IP address         Stratum Poll Reach LastRx Last sample
^? ntp-old.corp.example           0  10     0     -     +0ns[   +0ns] +/-    0ns

effects.finding: The only source is ntp-old.corp.example: '?' and Reach 0, so chronyd has had no reply from it at all.

tracking.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

showConf.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

effects.finding: chrony.conf still names the time server retired last month.

smbLog.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

smbd[3114]: Kerberos: ticket from lee@CORP.EXAMPLE rejected: Clock skew too great

editConf.label: sed -i 's/ntp-old/ntp1/' /etc/chrony.conf && echo 'server ntp2.corp.example iburst' >> /etc/chrony.conf
editConf.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

effects.log: chrony.conf names the two current time servers. chronyd reads it when it starts.

restart.label: systemctl restart chronyd
restart.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

then.log: chronyd started, reached ntp1 with iburst, and makestep 1 3 stepped the clock 580 s on its first update.

else.log: chronyd restarted with the same retired server: still nothing to sync to.

addRuntime.label: chronyc add server ntp1.corp.example iburst
addRuntime.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

effects.output:
[root@files2 ~]# chronyc add server ntp1.corp.example iburst
200 OK

effects.log: chronyd has a reachable source, but it has been up for 41 days, so makestep 1 3 no longer applies: it slews the 580 s at most one twelfth, about two hours.

makestep.label: chronyc makestep
makestep.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

then.log: chronyd jumped the clock by the correction it was slewing: the clock is right.
Nothing to step: chronyd has no selected source, so it has no correction to apply.

dateSet.label: date -s "$(ssh admin1 date)"
dateSet.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

effects.output:
[root@files2 ~]# date -s "$(ssh admin1 date)"
Sat Nov 14 10:0x:xx AM PST 2026

effects.log: The clock was set by hand from another server; chronyd still has no source, so it drifts again and the next snapshot restore repeats this.

widenSkew.label: sed -i '/libdefaults/a clockskew = 3600' /etc/krb5.conf
widenSkew.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

effects.log: Kerberos on files2 now accepts messages up to an hour old: logins work, and the replay protection the five-minute limit gives is gone.

writeup.question: For the incident record: why logins failed, what you found in chrony, and why your fix will hold after the next restore or reboot.

parts.label: Cause
parts.criteria: Names the clock about 580 s slow after the snapshot restore, past Kerberos's 300 s default limit, and chrony unable to correct it because its only source is the retired server.
parts.modelAnswer: The restore put the clock back almost ten minutes; Kerberos rejects anything over five minutes; chronyc sources showed only ntp-old with '?' and Reach 0.

parts.label: Evidence
parts.criteria: Uses timedatectl, chronyc sources or tracking and the chrony.conf server lines before changing anything.
parts.modelAnswer: timedatectl said not synchronized; chronyc sources showed ^? ntp-old, Reach 0; chrony.conf still named ntp-old.

parts.label: Fix
parts.criteria: Puts the current servers in chrony.conf and restarts chronyd (makestep 1 3 steps at start), or adds them and runs chronyc makestep, with the file fixed; never widens the Kerberos skew or sets the clock by hand as the fix; checks sources and a login.
parts.modelAnswer: Replaced the server line with ntp1 and ntp2, restarted chronyd so its first update stepped the clock under makestep 1 3; chronyc sources showed ^* ntp1, Reach 377; smbclient -k listed the share.

noProgress.rationale: Closing while logins fail leaves finance and payroll without the share; it is never a safe outcome.

skewWidened.label: Logins back, a control weakened
skewWidened.narrative: Logins work because Kerberos on files2 now accepts messages an hour old, which removes the replay protection the five-minute limit gives.

fixed.narrative: chrony.conf names the current servers, chronyd is synced and the clock was stepped; logins work and will keep working after the next restore.

expertPath.text: timedatectl: not synchronized. chronyc sources: only ^? ntp-old, Reach 0.
grep the server lines in /etc/chrony.conf: it still names the retired server; makestep 1 3 is set.
Replace it with ntp1 and ntp2, systemctl restart chronyd: the first update steps the clock.
chronyc sources (^* ntp1, 377) and smbclient -k; record it, and suggest checking chrony after every snapshot restore.

fixed.headline: Good: synced and stepped
fixed.body: You read chrony's own view, fixed the source where chronyd reads it, and used makestep's start-up step instead of waiting hours for a slew.

fixedGaps.headline: Logins back, with gaps
fixedGaps.body: Logins work. The criteria show the gap: a clock set by hand drifts again, and a source added with chronyc add is gone at the next restart.

skewWidened.headline: A control weakened
skewWidened.body: The five-minute Kerberos limit is replay protection. The clock was wrong; fix the clock.

stillFailing.headline: Closed too soon
stillFailing.body: chronyc makestep has nothing to step until chronyd has a source it can reach. Check chronyc sources for a '*'.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Kerberos rejects a clock more than 300 s off; the restore left files2 580 s slow. chronyc sources shows why chrony never corrected it: its only server is retired (?, Reach 0). Fix chrony.conf and restart chronyd: makestep 1 3 steps on the first updates after start. A chronyc add without the file, a date -s, or a wider clockskew each leaves a problem behind.
